statement_source_and_scope_match: NSW published §1 Open Question 1 and §2 define the exact three-machine unit-job makespan problem. DW §1 independently singles out m=3; BDM §5 retains the fixed-machine ordinary-precedence gap. Integral-slot formulation is equivalent to nonpreemptive unit-job scheduling: fix machine orders in a feasible schedule and left-justify using longest paths in the combined precedence/order DAG. Binary search on T in [0,n] converts feasibility to optimum makespan; no release dates, communication delays, OR constraints or machine-dependent durations are introduced.
proposed_statement_text:
Let $G=(J,E)$ be a directed acyclic graph with $n$ vertices, one for each job, and let $T$ be a nonnegative integer supplied in binary. Every job takes exactly one unit of time on any of three identical processors. A job must finish before any of its successors begins. Jobs cannot be interrupted; each processor runs at most one job at a time; all jobs are available at time zero subject to the precedence constraints.

Decide whether there is a schedule that completes all jobs by time $T$. Equivalently, does there exist a map $s:J\to\{0,\ldots,T-1\}$ such that

$$
s(v)\ge s(u)+1\quad((u,v)\in E),\qquad
|\{j\in J:s(j)=t\}|\le3\quad(0\le t<T)?
$$

Determine the computational complexity of this decision problem, conventionally written $P3\mid\mathrm{prec},p_j=1\mid C_{\max}$. In particular, is it solvable by a deterministic algorithm polynomial in the input length, or can NP-completeness be established under polynomial-time many-one reductions? No dichotomy between these outcomes is assumed. The number of processors is fixed at three, while the job graph and deadline are unrestricted input. The goal is exact feasibility, not an approximation to the minimum completion time.
applied_significance: Precedence edges represent dependencies between computational tasks or project activities. Fixing three identical processors removes machine heterogeneity and numerical processing-time encoding, isolating the algorithmic difficulty created by dependencies and limited parallelism. Resolving exact tractability would clarify when an optimal schedule can be computed efficiently for this basic resource-allocation model.

closest_existing_or_new_entries.difference: Asks for a better-than-two approximation with arbitrary machine-dependent processing times and no precedence constraints; candidate asks exact complexity with three identical processors and unit jobs.
Max-min item allocation with arbitrary values is not precedence scheduling.
Strongly polynomial simplex pivoting concerns linear programming and arithmetic magnitudes, not exact discrete scheduling.
Unique Games is a distinct general hardness conjecture; conditional approximation hardness for growing machine counts does not settle this exact fixed-machine question.
